The Chief Executive’s report for May was tabled. Key points highlighted:

- **Operational Performance:** May saw an average of 98.2% of supply zones at the target pressure. There were 14 unplanned supply interruptions of over 12 minutes, of which 3 were over 3 hours. The longest interruption was 5 hours 40 minutes in the Bloxham area on 18 May, caused by a third-party strike on a trunk main.
- **Customer Complaints:** 212 written complaints were received in May, a slight increase from 189 in April. The majority related to billing queries following the implementation of the new system. The Head of Customer Services was in attendance to provide detail under item 6.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley serves_as Operations Director. Record status: current.

**5. Financial Report (May 2023)**

Ms. Raman presented the financial position for the month ended 31 May 2023.

- **Operating Expenditure:** Year-to-date operating expenditure is £24.6m, which is 1.1% above the profiled budget. The overspend is primarily attributable to increased electricity costs at the two main pumping stations, which were 3.4% higher than forecast.
- **Capital Programme:** The capital programme spend to date is £8.2m against a profiled budget of £9.1m. The slippage is largely due to the delayed start of the Cherwell Valley pipeline rehabilitation project, which is now expected to commence on site in July.
- **Revenue:** Revenue from water charges is £31.4m, in line with the forecast.
- **Bad Debt Provision:** The provision for doubtful debts has been increased by £150,000 to reflect the ongoing impact of the cost of living on a small cohort of customers. The Board noted the increase.

**Decision:** The Board approved the May financial report and the revised bad debt provision.

**6. Customer Services Update – Billing System Implementation**

Mr. Cole attended the meeting for this item. He reported that the new billing system, which went live on 17 April, had encountered a number of data migration issues. These had resulted in some customers receiving incorrect bills, primarily duplicate invoices for the same period.

- Mr. Cole confirmed that a remediation plan had been put in place. As of 30 May, 1,847 duplicate bills had been identified, and 1,402 had been corrected.
- The remaining corrections are expected to be completed by 16 June.
- The Board noted the level of complaints and asked Mr. Cole to provide a further update at the July meeting.
- A meeting had been held with the Drinking Water Inspectorate (DWI) on 6 September to discuss the outcome of the annual compliance assessment. The DWI had confirmed that no formal enforcement action was required for 2022-23.
- The Chief Executive had written to all customers in the areas affected by the June billing errors, apologising for the inconvenience and confirming the remedial action taken.
- Mr. Fletcher reported that he had been invited to speak at the Water UK annual conference in November on the topic of community engagement in reservoir management. The Board noted this.

**3. Operations Report – August 2023**

Dr. Hartley presented the operational performance report for August.

- **Supply and Demand:** Total water supplied in August was 11,842 megalitres, which was 2.3% above the forecast. The increase was attributed to the prolonged dry spell during the first three weeks of the month.
- **Leakage:** The rolling 12-month leakage figure was 148 megalitres per day, which is 4 megalitres per day above the target. Dr. Hartley noted that the additional leakage was concentrated in the Cherwell Valley area, where the pipework is older and the ground conditions have been challenging.
- **Water Quality:** All 46 routine samples taken from the distribution network in August were compliant with the relevant standards. One sample taken from a service reservoir had failed the coliform test; the reservoir had been taken out of service for inspection and cleaning, and a repeat sample had been compliant.
- **Staff Updates:** The two graduate engineers appointed in June had both commenced employment in August. One had been assigned to the Network Control Team and the other to the Asset Planning Team.

Mr. Whitfield provided additional detail on the network control function. He confirmed that the telemetry system upgrade, which had been scheduled for completion in July, had encountered minor software configuration issues. These had now been resolved. He reported that the system was operating as expected and that the control room had successfully managed two unplanned burst mains during August without any loss of supply to customers.

**4. Reservoir Storage Policy – Proposal for Adoption**

Dr. Hartley introduced a paper proposing the adoption of a new Reservoir Storage Policy. She explained that the policy had been developed in response to a recommendation from the internal audit of the reservoir safety management system, which had been completed in March 2023.

James Whitfield serves_as Network Control Manager. Record status: current.

- The policy sets out the minimum storage levels for each of the company’s eight service reservoirs, taking into account seasonal variations and the need to maintain resilience in the event of a major supply interruption.
- It also defines the triggers for implementing demand management measures, such as hosepipe bans, and the process for escalating decisions to the Board.
- Dr. Hartley noted that the policy had been developed in consultation with the reservoir engineers and the Environment Agency.

Mr. Whitfield spoke in support of the proposal. He said that the policy would provide clear guidance for the Network Control Team, who currently rely on a combination of operational experience and ad-hoc instructions when storage levels fall. He confirmed that the control room had already begun using the draft policy as a reference during the recent dry spell.

The Board discussed the storage level triggers. Ms. Raman asked whether the policy included any financial implications. Dr. Hartley confirmed that the policy did not require any additional capital expenditure, but that the implementation of demand management measures could have a revenue impact in a drought year. This was noted.

**Decision:** The Board resolved to adopt the Reservoir Storage Policy, effective from 1 October 2023. The policy will be reviewed annually, or earlier if there are significant changes to the reservoir infrastructure.

**Action 23/55:** Dr. Hartley to circulate the final version of the Reservoir Storage Policy to the Board and to ensure that it is included in the operational procedures manual. Due: 29 September 2023.

**3. EMCC Planning Approval – Barlborough Pumping Station**

Mr. Okafor presented an update on the planning application for the new pumping station at Barlborough.

- The application had been submitted to East Midlands County Council (EMCC) in July 2023.
- On 30 October 2023, EMCC granted planning approval for the construction of the pumping station and the associated access road.
- The approval was subject to a number of conditions, including a landscaping plan, a construction traffic management plan, and a noise assessment to be submitted to EMCC for approval prior to commencement of works.
- The Environment Agency had raised no objections, subject to the inclusion of a surface water drainage scheme in accordance with the submitted flood risk assessment.

Mr. Okafor noted that the planning approval represented a significant milestone for the project, which would improve resilience in the north-east of the supply area. The pumping station would enable the transfer of up to 12 megalitres per day from the Derwent Valley Aquifer to the Barlborough service reservoir, reducing reliance on the Trent abstraction during peak demand periods.

**Decision:** The Board noted the planning approval and authorised Mr. Okafor to proceed with the procurement of the main construction contract.

**2. Demand forecast review 2024–2030**

Mr. Ashworth presented the annual demand forecast review for the period 2024–2030. The forecast had been prepared by the Asset Management team in consultation with the Water Quality and Operations teams.

Key points:

- **Current demand:** Average daily demand for 2023 was 312 megalitres per day (Ml/d), compared with 308 Ml/d in 2022. The increase was attributed to a wetter than average autumn and increased leakage during the cold spell in early December.
- **Forecast growth:** The forecast assumed a 1.2% per annum increase in domestic consumption, driven largely by new housing developments in the Chesterfield and Bolsover areas. Commercial demand was expected to remain flat.
- **Peak demand:** The summer peak demand forecast for 2024 was 385 Ml/d, which was within the current supply capacity of 410 Ml/d, assuming no major outages.
- **Uncertainty:** Mr. Ashworth noted that the forecast carried a higher degree of uncertainty than usual, owing to the variability in weather patterns and the potential for a second consecutive dry summer. He recommended that the forecast be reviewed again in June, following the publication of the Environment Agency’s seasonal outlook.

The Board discussed the implications of the forecast for the capital programme and for the company’s performance commitments. Mr. Whitfield noted that the forecast would be used to inform the development of the next business plan submission to the regulator.

Robert Ashworth serves_as Asset Management Director. Record status: current.

**Decision:** The Board approved the demand forecast for 2024–2030 as the basis for operational planning and capital investment decisions.

**3. AMR Metering Pilot – recommendations for further roll-out**

Mr. Whitfield introduced the item, explaining that the Board had previously agreed to a pilot of automatic meter reading (AMR) technology in two areas of the supply zone. The pilot had been running for nine months, and the results were now available for consideration.

Ms. Foster presented the findings of the pilot evaluation. The pilot had involved the installation of 4,200 AMR meters in the Dronfield and Wingerworth areas, covering a mix of domestic and small commercial properties.

Key results:

- **Data quality:** The AMR meters had provided daily consumption data for 98.7% of connected properties, compared with the 60% to 70% read rates achieved through the traditional manual reading programme.
- **Leakage detection:** The pilot had identified 23 customer-side leaks that had not been previously reported. Of these, 18 had been repaired within the pilot period, with an estimated saving of 1.4 Ml/d.
- **Customer engagement:** A survey of pilot participants found that 71% were satisfied with the new meters, and 64% said they had used the consumption data to change their water usage behaviour.
- **Cost:** The average cost per meter, including installation and data management, was £142, which was 12% higher than the original estimate. The higher cost was attributed to the need for additional communications equipment in areas with poor mobile coverage.
- Action 14/012 (Ms. Foster): The draft financial model for the 2025–2030 business plan had been circulated to Board members on 8 March. Ms. Foster confirmed that the model would be presented for approval at the April meeting.

Mr. Whitfield invited Ms. Foster to complete the presentation of the pilot results.

Ms. Foster confirmed the remaining findings:

- **Customer-side leak repairs:** Of the 23 customer-side leaks identified, 18 had been repaired within the pilot period. The remaining five were awaiting repair appointments at the time of the evaluation.
- **Operational efficiency:** The pilot had reduced the requirement for manual meter reading visits by an estimated 1,900 hours per year across the two pilot areas.
- **Data management:** The AMR data had been integrated into the company’s existing customer billing system without significant issues. A small number of data transmission gaps had been observed in the Wingerworth area, attributed to topography.

Ms. Foster presented the recommendation to proceed with a phased roll-out of a further 18,000 AMR meters across the supply zone over the next two years. The phased approach would allow the company to manage the higher-than-expected installation costs and to address the communications coverage issues identified in the pilot.

Sarah Coles serves_as Customer Services Manager. Record status: current.

**Discussion:**

Mr. Okafor noted that the operational benefits of the pilot had been significant, particularly in the early identification of customer-side leaks. He supported the phased roll-out, subject to a review of the communications equipment specification.

- The number of complaints resolved within the target of 10 working days was 91%, compared with the target of 95%. Ms. Coles explained that the shortfall was due to a small number of complex cases relating to the new billing system, which had now been resolved.

Mr. Whitfield invited Ms. Foster to complete the presentation of the pilot results.

Ms. Foster confirmed the remaining findings:

- **Customer-side leak repairs:** Of the 23 customer-side leaks identified, 18 had been repaired within the pilot period. The remaining five were awaiting repair appointments at the time of the evaluation.
- **Operational efficiency:** The pilot had reduced the requirement for manual meter reading visits by an estimated 1,900 hours per year across the two pilot areas.
- **Data management:** The AMR data had been integrated into the company’s existing customer billing system without significant issues. A small number of data transmission gaps had been observed in the Wingerworth area, attributed to topography.

The phased approach would allow the company to manage the higher-than-expected installation costs and to address the communications coverage issues identified in the pilot.

The Chair invited Mr. Fenwick and Ms. Donovan to present the item, referencing the letter from the WIC dated 24 January 2025, which had been summarised in the Chair’s report earlier in the meeting.

- Ms. Donovan confirmed that the Commission’s compliance audit, conducted in October 2024, had focused on three areas: leakage reporting accuracy, customer complaint handling timescales, and the management of the company’s Priority Services Register.
- The overall outcome was a rating of “Broadly Compliant”, with two minor recommendations and one area of concern requiring a formal action plan.
- The area of concern related to the verification of Priority Services Register entries. - The two recommendations were: (a) that the company should publish its annual leakage performance data in a more accessible format on its website, and (b) that complaint handling correspondence should include a clearer reference to the customer’s right to escalate to the WIC.

**Proposed Response:**

- Mr. Okafor confirmed that the lapsed Priority Services Register records had already been re-verified during February 2025. A full re-verification of all 500 sampled records was completed on 21 February 2025, with no further gaps identified.
- A revised internal audit schedule would be introduced from April 2025, moving Priority Services Register verification to a 12-month cycle, exceeding the Commission’s minimum requirement.
- The Customer Services team would update the standard complaint correspondence template by 30 April 2025 to include the escalation wording recommended by the Commission.
- The Communications team would work with Mr. Fenwick’s team to publish the annual leakage performance data in a revised format, with a target date of 30 June 2025.

documents.title: EMWA Demand Forecast Report
documents.content:
The growth rates reflect the following factors:

- **Trent Supply Zone (3.2%):** The primary driver is the phased completion of the North-West Quadrant Development (1,200 new homes by end of 2025), along with a 4% increase in non-household demand from the new logistics hub near Junction 24. The growth rate is the highest among the zones, and the OPG has flagged this as a key risk area for network capacity.
- **Severn Lowlands (1.8%):** Growth is driven by a steady increase in commercial demand, particularly in the food processing sector. Household demand is forecast to remain flat.
- **Wreake Valley (1.7%):** Growth is modest, with no major new connections planned until the Wreake Business Park is fully consented. The forecast assumes a 0.5% reduction in household consumption due to existing water efficiency programmes.

**4. Peak Demand Forecast for Trent Supply Zone**

The peak demand forecast is the primary focus of this report, given the capacity constraints identified in the 2024 Network Capacity Review. The table below presents the forecast peak demand for the Trent Supply Zone for the summer of 2025, alongside the comparable 2024 figure.

**Table 2: Peak Demand Forecast – Trent Supply Zone (TSZ)**

| Parameter | 2024 Actual (ML/d) | 2025 Forecast (ML/d) | Change (%) | Status |
|-----------|--------------------|----------------------|------------|--------|
| Peak Day Demand | 684 | 720 | 5.3% | Current |
| 7-day Average Peak | 655 | 685 | 4.6% | Current |
| Time of Peak | Mid-July | Mid-July (estimated) | – | Estimated |

The EMWA demand forecast 2025 states that Trent Supply Zone has peak demand of 720 ML/d. Record status: current. This figure represents the maximum daily demand expected during a dry summer day, assuming no prolonged heatwave (defined as more than five consecutive days above 28°C). The forecast is based on a statistical analysis of the last five years of demand data, adjusted for the growth factors outlined in Section 3.

The peak demand figure is a **current** controlled entry in the OPG demand database and will be used as the reference value for the 2025 network capacity planning cycle. The previous forecast, issued in November 2024, estimated a peak of 705 ML/d; this has been superseded by the current figure following an upward revision of the housing completion schedule for the North-West Quadrant.

**5. Methodology and Assumptions**

The forecast was prepared using the following methodology:

1. **Baseline adjustment:** The 2024 actual demand data was reviewed for anomalies (e.g., leakage events, supply restrictions) and adjusted to reflect a "normal" dry year.
2. **Growth factor application:** Zone-level growth rates were applied, based on housing completions (from local planning authority data), non-household demand projections (from the OPG commercial team), and population projections (ONS mid-2023 estimates).
3. **Climate adjustment:** A +2% uplift was applied to the baseline peak demand to account for the effects of climate change, based on the Authority's Climate Impact Note 2024/03. This uplift is within the range recommended by the Environment Agency.
4. **Peak day calculation:** The peak day demand was calculated by applying a zone-specific peaking factor (the ratio of peak day to average dry year demand) to the adjusted baseline. For TSZ, the peaking factor is 1.69, which is consistent with recent years.

Assumptions and caveats:

- The forecast assumes **no major supply interruptions** (e.g., treatment works outages) during the peak period.
- The forecast assumes **normal summer weather** (i.e., a "dry year" but not an extreme drought). A 1-in-10-year drought would increase peak demand by approximately 4%.
- The forecast does not include the effect of any new demand-side management measures beyond those already committed in the 2024/25 Water Efficiency Action Plan.

EMWA Demand Forecast Report 2025

**Document reference:** OPG/DFR/2025/02
**Issue date:** 15 January 2025
**Prepared by:** Operations Planning Group (OPG), Asset Management Division
**Author:** J. R. Whitmore, Senior Demand Analyst
**Approved by:** M. Okafor, OPG Lead

---

**1. Purpose and Scope**

This report presents the 2025 annual demand forecast for the East Mercia Water Authority (EMWA) supply zones. The forecast updates the November 2024 interim projection and provides the reference demand values for the 2025 network capacity planning cycle, the Water Resources Management Plan annual review, and the leakage reduction programme targets.

The forecast covers the following supply zones:

- Leicester Supply Zone (LSZ)
- Trentside Supply Zone (TSZ)
- Vale of Belvoir Supply Zone (VBZ)

All demand figures are expressed in megalitres per day (ML/d) unless otherwise stated. The forecast horizon is the calendar year 2025, with peak demand values provided for the summer peak period (June to August).

---

**2. Executive Summary**

Total average dry year demand across all EMWA zones is forecast at 612 ML/d for 2025, an increase of 1.4% against the 2024 outturn. Peak day demand for the Authority as a whole is forecast at 1,028 ML/d.

The headline figure for network capacity planning is the peak demand for the Leicester Supply Zone. The EMWA demand forecast 2025 states that Leicester Supply Zone has peak demand of 480 ML/d. Record status: current. This is a **current** controlled entry in the OPG demand database and will be used as the reference value for the 2025 network capacity planning cycle.

The previous forecast, issued in November 2024, estimated a peak of 705 ML/d for LSZ; that figure has been superseded by the current value following the upward revision of the housing completion schedule for the North-West Quadrant. The revision reflects an additional 1,240 dwellings now expected to be completed by June 2025, together with a higher than anticipated take-up of non-household connections at the Meridian Business Park extension.

---

**3. Demand Baseline and Growth**

**3.1 Historical Outturn**

Table 1 summarises the actual demand outturn for the period 2020 to 2024, expressed as average dry year demand and peak day demand.

| Year | LSZ Avg Dry Year (ML/d) | LSZ Peak Day (ML/d) | TSZ Avg Dry Year (ML/d) | TSZ Peak Day (ML/d) | VBZ Avg Dry Year (ML/d) | VBZ Peak Day (ML/d) |
|------|--------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|
| 2020 | 428 | 710 | 312 | 527 | 96 | 152 |
| 2021 | 431 | 715 | 315 | 531 | 97 | 154 |
| 2022 | 439 | 729 | 319 | 538 | 99 | 157 |
| 2023 | 445 | 739 | 322 | 543 | 100 | 159 |
| 2024 | 451 | 748 | 326 | 549 | 101 | 161 |

*Table 1: Historical demand outturn by zone, 2020–2024*

The 2024 outturn for LSZ was affected by two periods of supply restriction in July (a burst on the Raw Dykes trunk main and a planned outage at the Cropston treatment works). These events are estimated to have suppressed recorded demand by approximately 2.1 ML/d on the affected days. The outturn has been adjusted to reflect a normal dry year.

**3.2 Growth Rates**

Growth rates for 2025 were derived from the following sources:

- **Housing completions:** Local planning authority data for Leicester, Blaby, Oadby and Wigston, and Charnwood. A total of 2,180 dwellings are expected to complete in LSZ during 2025, of which 1,240 are in the North-West Quadrant (Anstey, Glenfield, and Kirby Muxloe areas).
- **Non-household demand:** OPG commercial team projections, based on known connection applications and sector growth. Notable additions include the Meridian Business Park extension (estimated 3.8 ML/d at full build-out) and a new data centre at Grove Park (estimated 1.2 ML/d from Q3 2025).
- **Population projections:** ONS mid-2023 estimates, with a 0.6% annual growth rate applied to the LSZ resident population.

## 4. Peak Demand and Climate Considerations

**4.1 Peak Day Demand**

Peak day demand is the principal driver of network capacity requirements. Table 2 presents the peak day demand forecast for 2025, together with the planning assumptions used.

| Year | LSZ Peak Day (ML/d) | TSZ Peak Day (ML/d) | VBZ Peak Day (ML/d) | Peak Day / Avg Dry Year Ratio (LSZ) |
|------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------|
| 2025 | 756 | 553 | 163 | 1.68 |
| 2026 | 762 | 558 | 165 | 1.68 |
| 2027 | 768 | 563 | 167 | 1.68 |
| 2028 | 774 | 568 | 169 | 1.68 |
| 2029 | 780 | 573 | 171 | 1.68 |
| 2030 | 786 | 578 | 173 | 1.68 |

*Table 2: Peak day demand forecast by zone, 2025–2030*

The peak day ratio of 1.68 reflects the average of the last five years, during which the ratio has remained stable at between 1.66 and 1.70. The peak day forecast for 2025 assumes a hot, dry summer comparable to 2022, with three consecutive days above 30°C in late July. It does not include any allowance for demand suppression through temporary use restrictions.

**4.2 Climate Impact Notes**

The 2025 forecast incorporates the following climate-related adjustments:

- **Summer temperature:** The Met Office seasonal outlook for summer 2025 indicates a 55% probability of above-average temperatures. A 1°C increase above the 1991–2020 baseline is associated with a peak day demand uplift of approximately 4.5 ML/d across LSZ.
- **Soil moisture deficit:** The hydrological outlook for spring 2025 suggests a drier than average April and May. This increases garden watering demand earlier in the season. An allowance of 1.8 ML/d has been added to the May average dry year figure for LSZ.
- **Evaporation and reservoir losses:** The Cropston and Swithland reservoirs are expected to lose an additional 0.6 ML/d to evaporation during the summer months compared with the long-term average. This is reflected in the supply-demand balance rather than in the demand forecast itself.
- **Winter recharge:** Groundwater levels in the Sherwood Sandstone aquifer remain below the long-term average following the dry autumn of 2024. This does not directly affect demand but is relevant to supply-side planning.

The climate adjustments are consistent with the approach used in the 2024 forecast. No further revision is proposed at this stage, although the OPG will review the position following the April rainfall data.
